transcript.heading: News Report One (British Male)
paras: A university in Scotland has become the first in the United Kingdom to offer a fully accredited degree program in magic and occult studies. The four-year bachelor's program, which will begin accepting students next September, will cover the history of magic, Western esotericism, pagan studies, and the role of the occult in literature and popular culture. University officials say the program is designed to provide serious academic study of a subject that has influenced art, religion, and philosophy for thousands of years but has rarely been treated as a legitimate field of scholarly inquiry. The curriculum will include courses on ancient mystery religions, medieval witchcraft, alchemy, modern occult movements, and the representation of magic in film and fiction. The program has already received more than 300 inquiries from prospective students, surprising university administrators who initially expected the course to appeal to a small niche audience. While some critics have mocked the program, scholars of religious studies have defended it, noting that understanding alternative spiritual traditions is important for cultural literacy. The university plans to invite practicing magicians and pagans as guest speakers to provide real-world perspectives on the subjects being studied.
Questions 1 and 2 are based on the news report you have just heard.
1. What is special about the new degree program at the Scottish university?
2. How have scholars of religious studies responded to the program?

transcript.heading: News Report Two (American Female)
paras: The world's first fully electric commercial aircraft completed its maiden voyage yesterday, flying for approximately 15 minutes over the Canadian city of Vancouver. The plane, which can carry up to nine passengers, is powered entirely by lithium-ion batteries and produces zero emissions during flight. The company behind the aircraft says the plane is designed for short-haul regional flights of up to 400 kilometers, which represents a significant portion of commercial air routes currently served by small propeller planes. The successful test flight was hailed as a major milestone in the development of sustainable aviation, an industry that accounts for approximately 2.5 percent of global carbon emissions. While larger electric passenger planes are still decades away due to battery weight limitations, company executives say smaller electric aircraft could begin commercial service as early as 2027. Several major airlines have already expressed interest in purchasing the planes for short regional routes. The aviation industry is also exploring other sustainable technologies, including hydrogen fuel cells and sustainable aviation fuels made from waste materials, but electric propulsion is seen as the most promising zero-emission solution for short flights.
Questions 3 to 5 are based on the news report you have just heard.
3. Where did the first fully electric commercial aircraft complete its maiden flight?
4. What is the maximum flight range of the new electric plane?
5. When do company executives expect smaller electric aircraft to begin commercial service?

transcript.heading: News Report Three (British Female)
paras: A new survey of 2,000 office workers has found that the average employee spends more than two hours each workday worrying about money, leading to reduced productivity and increased stress. The research, conducted by a financial wellness company, found that money concerns are the number one source of stress for working adults, ranking higher than job security, workload, and relationship issues. Nearly 60 percent of respondents reported that financial worries had affected their ability to concentrate at work, and approximately one in three said they had missed work due to stress related to financial problems. Younger workers between the ages of 18 and 34 reported the highest levels of financial stress, with student loan debt, housing costs, and credit card debt being the most common concerns. In response to these findings, a growing number of employers are beginning to offer financial wellness programs as part of their employee benefits packages, including access to financial advisors, budgeting workshops, and student loan repayment assistance. Human resources experts say that helping employees with financial stress not only improves worker well-being but also reduces turnover and increases overall productivity for the company.
Questions 6 and 7 are based on the news report you have just heard.
6. According to the survey, what is the number one source of stress for working adults?
7. What are more employers beginning to offer in response?

transcript.heading: Conversation One (American Female + American Male)
paras: Man (Chris): Hey, Ashley. Did you go to the career fair yesterday? I stopped by for about an hour, but it was so crowded I could barely talk to any recruiters.

Woman (Ashley): I did go, and I actually had a pretty good experience! I got there right when it opened at 10 AM, before it got too busy. I spoke to representatives from about six different companies.

Man: That's awesome. Did any of them seem particularly interesting? I'm looking for an internship for the summer, ideally in marketing or advertising. I'm graduating next year, so I really need some relevant work experience.

Woman: You should definitely talk to the people from the digital marketing agency—they were really friendly, and they said they have several summer internship positions available. They work with a lot of big clients, doing social media campaigns, content creation, and brand strategy. It sounds like a really dynamic place to work.

Man: That sounds perfect for me! Did they say what they're looking for in candidates? I have a little experience running social media for my fraternity, but I don't have any professional experience yet.

Woman: They said they're looking for people who are creative, have good communication skills, and are familiar with major social media platforms. They also mentioned that they value enthusiasm and a willingness to learn more than perfect grades or extensive experience. You should send them your resume—I think you'd be a strong candidate.
Man: I'll definitely do that. Did you pick up any business cards or brochures from them?

Woman: I did! I have a flyer with all the information, including the email address to send applications to. I can give it to you after class. The application deadline is February 15th, so you have about three weeks to put your materials together.
Man: That's great, I really appreciate that. What about you? Are you looking for an internship too? I thought you were already working part-time at that accounting firm.

Woman: I am still working there, but I'm actually looking for something in human resources after I graduate, so I was talking to a few companies that have HR training programs. I had a really good conversation with the recruiter from the healthcare company—they have a great rotational program where you get experience in several different departments.
Man: That sounds promising. Did you give them your resume?
Woman: Yes, and they said they'd be in touch to schedule an interview within the next couple of weeks. I'm trying not to get my hopes up too high, but I'm really excited about the possibility.
Man: Well, good luck! Let me know if you get an interview—I'd be happy to help you practice if you want.

Woman: Thanks, Chris! Same to you with the marketing internship. Let's both work on our applications this weekend. We can meet at the library to edit each other's resumes and cover letters if you want.
Man: That sounds like a plan. I'll text you later to set up a time.
Questions 8 to 11 are based on the conversation you have just heard.

9. What position is Chris looking for?
10. When is the application deadline for the marketing internship?

transcript.heading: Conversation Two (British Male + British Female)
paras: Woman (Rachel): Hi Tom. I just got back from the campus housing office, and I have some terrible news. They told me there's been a problem with my dorm room application for next year, and there's no space left in the residence halls.
Man (Tom): That's awful, Rachel! What are you going to do? You can't commute from your parents' house, can't you? That's over an hour and a half each way.

Woman: I know, that's impossible. I'd never make it to 8 AM classes on time. I'm going to have to look for an apartment off campus, but I'm really worried about the cost. Apartments in this city are so expensive.

Man: Actually, I've been thinking about moving off campus too. The dorms are getting more expensive every year, and I'm tired of sharing a bathroom with 20 other people. We could look for a place together if you want? If we get a two-bedroom apartment and split the rent and utilities, it would be cheaper than living in the dorms, probably.
Woman: Really? Would you actually want to be roommates with me? That would be amazing! But I've never rented an apartment before. Where do we even start?

Man: Me neither, but my cousin has lived in several apartments around here, and she gave me some advice last time I talked to her. First, we should figure out our budget—how much can you afford to pay each month, including rent, utilities, internet, and groceries?
Woman: I can probably afford around 500 pounds per month, maximum. I have some savings from my summer job, but I don't want to spend all of it on rent.

Man: That's about what I was thinking too. If we can find a place for 800-900 pounds a month total, that would be perfect. We should also think about location—we need to be close to campus or near a bus line that goes directly to the university. I don't have a car, do you?

Woman: No, I don't either. So being on a bus route is essential. We should also look for a place that has laundry facilities in the building or at least in the apartment—going to the laundromat every week would be such a hassle.
Man: Agreed. And I'd really like a place with a decent kitchen. I'm tired of eating dining hall food, and I want to start cooking my own meals. It's cheaper and healthier anyway.
Woman: That sounds wonderful. When should we start looking? I've heard that good apartments near campus get rented out really quickly for the next academic year.

Man: Let's start browsing listings online tonight. There are a few websites specifically for student housing in this area. We can make a list of places that look good and then call to schedule viewings for this weekend. We should also ask some of our friends if they know of anyone looking for a roommate or if their apartments have any vacancies.
Woman: Great idea. I'll also post on the student Facebook group to see if anyone knows of available places. Fingers crossed we can find something nice that's not too expensive!
Man: Don't worry, I'm sure we will. It'll be way better than living in the dorms—we'll have our own space, no more quiet hours, and we won't have to eat that terrible cafeteria food anymore!

transcript.heading: Passage One (American Male)
paras: The human brain contains approximately 86 billion neurons, or nerve cells, connected by trillions of synapses that allow them to communicate with each other. This incredibly complex organ controls everything we do—from breathing and moving to thinking, feeling, and remembering. Despite decades of research, scientists are still discovering new information about how the brain works and how we can keep it healthy throughout our lives.

One of the most important discoveries in recent years is the concept of neuroplasticity—the brain's ability to reorganize itself by forming new neural connections throughout life. Contrary to the old belief that the brain becomes fixed and unchanging after childhood, research now shows that the brain continues to adapt and evolve well into old age. When we learn new skills, practice activities, or even change our thought patterns, we create new pathways in the brain, strengthening certain connections while weakening others. This is why people can recover from brain injuries, learn new languages at any age, and change long-standing habits.

To keep our brains healthy and functioning well, experts recommend several key strategies. First, regular physical exercise is not just good for our bodies—it's also one of the best things we can do for our brains. Exercise increases blood flow to the brain, encourages the growth of new brain cells, and has been shown to improve memory and cognitive function while reducing the risk of age-related cognitive decline. Even moderate exercise like brisk walking for 30 minutes a day can have significant benefits.

Second, staying mentally active is crucial. Just as our muscles need exercise to stay strong, our brains need stimulation to stay sharp. Activities like reading, solving puzzles, learning a musical instrument, taking classes, or engaging in meaningful conversations all help maintain brain health by creating new neural connections. The key is to keep challenging yourself with new and interesting activities rather than doing the same things every day.

Third, getting enough quality sleep is essential for brain health. While we sleep, our brains consolidate memories from the day and clear out waste products that accumulate during waking hours. Chronic sleep deprivation has been linked to poorer memory, reduced decision-making abilities, and an increased risk of developing neurodegenerative diseases later in life. Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep per night for optimal brain function.

Other factors that contribute to brain health include eating a balanced diet rich in fruits, vegetables, whole grains, and healthy fats; managing stress through practices like meditation or deep breathing; maintaining social connections with friends and family; and avoiding harmful substances like excessive alcohol and tobacco. Taking care of our brain health is important at every age, as it affects our ability to work, learn, maintain relationships, and enjoy life.

transcript.heading: Passage Two (British Female)
paras: The term "social media" refers to websites and applications that allow users to create and share content or participate in social networking. What started as platforms primarily for connecting with friends and sharing personal updates has evolved into a global phenomenon that affects nearly every aspect of modern life, from how we communicate and get our news to how businesses market their products and how political campaigns are run.

As of 2025, over 4.8 billion people around the world use social media, spending an average of two and a half hours per day on these platforms. The most popular platforms have billions of users each, offering features ranging from photo and video sharing to live streaming, messaging, and professional networking. Social media has transformed communication, making it possible to stay connected with friends and family across the globe instantly and at no cost. It has also given ordinary people a platform to share their opinions, showcase their talents, and build communities around shared interests, hobbies, and causes.

Businesses have embraced social media as a powerful marketing tool, allowing them to reach target audiences directly, engage with customers, and build brand awareness at a fraction of the cost of traditional advertising. Many companies now employ entire teams dedicated to managing their social media presence, and influencer marketing—paying individuals with large social media followings to promote products—has become a multi-billion dollar industry.

However, social media also has significant downsides that have caused growing concern among researchers, parents, and policymakers. One major issue is the impact on mental health, particularly among young people. Numerous studies have linked heavy social media use to increased rates of anxiety, depression, loneliness, and poor body image, especially among teenage girls. The curated, idealized versions of life that people often present on social media can lead to unhealthy comparisons and feelings of inadequacy.

Another concern is the spread of misinformation and fake news on social media platforms. Because content can be shared instantly with millions of people without going through traditional fact-checking processes, false information can spread rapidly, sometimes with serious real-world consequences. Social media has also been criticized for creating echo chambers, where users are primarily exposed to opinions and viewpoints similar to their own, reinforcing existing beliefs and reducing exposure to diverse perspectives.

Cyberbullying—harassment that takes place online—is another serious problem, affecting approximately one in three young people. Unlike traditional bullying, cyberbullying can follow victims into their homes, making it difficult to escape. Issues around privacy, data collection, and the addictive nature of social media platforms, which are designed to keep users engaged for as long as possible, have also come under increasing scrutiny.

As social media continues to evolve and play an increasingly central role in society, finding a healthy balance and developing digital literacy skills—learning to think critically about what we see online, protect our privacy, and use these tools in ways that enhance rather than detract from our well-being—has become an essential skill for navigating the modern world.

transcript.heading: Passage Three (American Female)
paras: The global food system is responsible for approximately one-third of all greenhouse gas emissions, making dietary choices one of the most significant ways that individuals can impact the environment. While food production affects the environment in many ways, including deforestation, water use, pollution from fertilizers, and transportation emissions, the production of meat and dairy products has a particularly outsized environmental footprint.

Beef production is by far the most resource-intensive food, requiring enormous amounts of land, water, and feed to produce relatively small amounts of protein. Producing one kilogram of beef generates approximately 60 kilograms of greenhouse gas emissions—more than driving a car for 250 kilometers. Cattle farming is also a major driver of deforestation, particularly in the Amazon rainforest, where vast areas of forest are cleared to create pasture land and grow feed crops for cattle. Lamb and goat production also have high environmental impacts, though not quite as high as beef.

Other animal products have lower but still significant footprints. Pork and poultry production generate fewer emissions per kilogram than beef, but still considerably more than plant-based protein sources like beans, lentils, and tofu. Dairy production, including milk, cheese, and yogurt, also contributes substantially to greenhouse gas emissions and water use, largely due to methane produced by cows and the resources needed to grow feed.

Plant-based foods generally have much lower environmental impacts across the board. Producing legumes like beans and lentils generates fewer than 2 kilograms of emissions per kilogram, uses dramatically less water, and requires a fraction of the land needed for meat production. Vegetables, fruits, whole grains, and nuts also have relatively low environmental footprints compared to animal products.

This doesn't necessarily mean that everyone needs to become vegan or vegetarian to make a difference. Even small changes in diet can add up to significant environmental benefits when adopted by large numbers of people. Experts suggest several practical approaches: participating in "Meatless Mondays" by going without meat one day a week, reducing portion sizes of meat when it is served, choosing chicken or fish instead of beef, and replacing some dairy products with plant-based alternatives like oat milk or soy milk.

Reducing food waste is another crucial aspect of sustainable eating. Approximately one-third of all food produced globally is wasted, representing a massive waste of the water, land, energy, and labor that went into producing it. Planning meals, buying only what you need, using leftovers, and composting food scraps can significantly reduce the environmental impact of our diets. Supporting local farmers by buying locally grown produce when possible can also reduce emissions from transportation and help strengthen local food systems.
